item.title: Evaluating Explanation Integrity in a Vision Language Model for Urban Perception
item.description: Transactions in GIS, Volume 30, Issue 8, December 2026.
item.dc:description: ABSTRACT Assessment of subjective experience of urban spaces is crucial for understanding how built environments shape our well‐being and behavior. Vision Language Models (VLMs) have shown promise in this area by accurately replicating human perception of urban spaces and offering both quantitative assessments and textual rationales for their evaluations. This paper examines how faithfully these rationales reflect visual evidence in images and whether they align with analytic explainability methods. Using semantic feature perturbation, we estimate the contributions of six visual categories (buildings, streets, people, vegetation, traffic, and sky) to VLM‐assigned scores across six perception dimensions (safe, beautiful, wealthy, lively, boring, and depressing). We compare these analytic attributions to the model's own explanations. While overall alignment is reasonable, we identify cases where rationales misrepresent visible features or contradict analytic attribution. These discrepancies highlight the limits of model‐derived explanations and underscore the need for rigorous evaluation of explanation integrity in multimodal models of urban perception.

ABSTRACT

Assessment of subjective experience of urban spaces is crucial for understanding how built environments shape our well-being and behavior. Vision Language Models (VLMs) have shown promise in this area by accurately replicating human perception of urban spaces and offering both quantitative assessments and textual rationales for their evaluations. This paper examines how faithfully these rationales reflect visual evidence in images and whether they align with analytic explainability methods. Using semantic feature perturbation, we estimate the contributions of six visual categories (buildings, streets, people, vegetation, traffic, and sky) to VLM-assigned scores across six perception dimensions (safe, beautiful, wealthy, lively, boring, and depressing). We compare these analytic attributions to the model's own explanations. While overall alignment is reasonable, we identify cases where rationales misrepresent visible features or contradict analytic attribution. These discrepancies highlight the limits of model-derived explanations and underscore the need for rigorous evaluation of explanation integrity in multimodal models of urban perception.

item.title: Quantifying Driving Visual Cognitive Friendliness on Urban Networks: A Multi‐Factor Framework Fusing 3D Spatial Mapping and Vision‐Language Models
item.description: Transactions in GIS, Volume 30, Issue 8, December 2026.
item.dc:description: ABSTRACT High visual cognitive workload in urban environments induces driver distraction, a primary catalyst for traffic collisions. However, current geospatial assessments struggle to simultaneously quantify macro‐geometric structures and micro‐semantic traffic elements across large‐scale networks. Addressing this gap, we introduce the Visual Cognitive Friendliness Index (VCFI) to evaluate the static infrastructure‐friendliness baseline of urban road networks. This GeoAI‐driven framework integrates panoptic segmentation, Vision‐Language Models (VLMs), and 3D geospatial mapping. Applied to over 31,000 street panoramas—serving as near‐surface earth observations—in Hong Kong, the framework accurately quantifies macro‐spatial geometries and micro‐level ground traffic markings. Validation against ground‐truth data demonstrates exceptional extraction robustness. Spatial analysis reveals a significant correlation between low‐VCFI segments and historical traffic blackspots, underscoring the infrastructure's impact on driving hazards. Furthermore, human‐in‐the‐loop experiments investigating cognitive consistency confirm a 92.31% agreement between algorithmic evaluations and human cognitive consensus. This scalable GeoAI methodology provides solid modeling support for urban infrastructure management, hazard mitigation, and location‐based intelligent transportation services.

ABSTRACT

High visual cognitive workload in urban environments induces driver distraction, a primary catalyst for traffic collisions. However, current geospatial assessments struggle to simultaneously quantify macro-geometric structures and micro-semantic traffic elements across large-scale networks. Addressing this gap, we introduce the Visual Cognitive Friendliness Index (VCFI) to evaluate the static infrastructure-friendliness baseline of urban road networks. This GeoAI-driven framework integrates panoptic segmentation, Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and 3D geospatial mapping. Applied to over 31,000 street panoramas—serving as near-surface earth observations—in Hong Kong, the framework accurately quantifies macro-spatial geometries and micro-level ground traffic markings. Validation against ground-truth data demonstrates exceptional extraction robustness. Spatial analysis reveals a significant correlation between low-VCFI segments and historical traffic blackspots, underscoring the infrastructure's impact on driving hazards. Furthermore, human-in-the-loop experiments investigating cognitive consistency confirm a 92.31% agreement between algorithmic evaluations and human cognitive consensus. This scalable GeoAI methodology provides solid modeling support for urban infrastructure management, hazard mitigation, and location-based intelligent transportation services.
